meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'колько'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: So much gum!
How much is it?
So much gum! Cool!

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'year' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I've been working here for four years.

examples.text: Это было давно, тридцать лет назад.
examples.trans: That was long ago, thirty years back.

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been working as mayor for four years now.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лушать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to listen', paired with 'послушать'.

examples.trans: Listen, Samson.
Yes, I'm listening.

examples.text: Слушай, Самсон, я тут подумал. Твой начальник — такой опытный специалист.
examples.trans: Listen, Samson, I've been thinking. Your boss is such an experienced specialist.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to see', paired with 'увидеть'.

examples.trans: I can see the toy car.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.
See the markers? They're from Japan!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'at, by; (у меня) I have', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I have a toy car.
He's at our place.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?
And this is for you. A toy car!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'everything, all; that's it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Everything's fine.
That's it, bye!

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: How is it in Hungary?
I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'рядок'). Formed with a diminutive/expressive Slavic suffix adding warmth or small scale. Common masculine noun meaning 'order' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Now let's go through everything in order.
Everything is in complete order.

examples.text: Теперь давай всё по порядку. Скажи мне, сколько ты им должна?
examples.trans: Now let's go through everything in order. Tell me, how much do you owe them?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'again', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: It's another trick.
Rain again.

examples.text: Нина, не слушай. Это опять обман.
examples.trans: Nina, don't listen. It's another trick.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'on, onto; for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Entered Russian via Polish 'kuchnia' and Middle High German 'küchen', ultimately from Late Latin 'coquina' (from 'coquere', to cook).

examples.trans: And the kitchen is over there.
We are sitting in the kitchen.

examples.text: Проходите, пожалуйста! Как видите, большой коридор, а там кухня.
examples.trans: Come on in, please! As you can see, a big hall, and the kitchen is over there.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Chef, I didn't take it.
I don't know.
I'm doing my homework.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.
And does the governor support you?

examples.text: Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('familiar, known').

examples.text: А знакомо ли тебе, Аркашка, слово педикюр?
examples.trans: And are you familiar, Arkashka, with the word pedicure?

examples.text: Я услышал в коридоре знакомый голос.
examples.trans: I heard a familiar voice in the corridor.
I will call acquaintances right now.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'my, mine', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Where's my toy car?
That's mine.
No. That's mine.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('first').

examples.trans: This is my first day.

examples.text: Ты не понимаешь с первого раза?
examples.trans: You don't understand the first time?

examples.text: Ты что, с первого раза не понимаешь?
examples.trans: What, you don't understand the first time?

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'chef' (head, leader, from Latin 'caput'); in Russian kitchen culture 'шеф' is the standard form of address for the executive head chef.

examples.trans: The chef is in the kitchen.
Chef, I didn't take it.
Cleverly thought out, boss!

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'читель'). Agent/instrument noun formed with the productive Slavic suffix '-тель' ('-er'). Common masculine noun meaning 'teacher' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Славик, ты слышишь, что учителя говорят?
examples.trans: Slavik, do you hear what the teachers are saying?

examples.text: Наш учитель истории очень интересно рассказывает.
examples.trans: Our history teacher tells stories very interestingly.

examples.text: Ты мой главный учитель и верный наставник.
examples.trans: You are my main teacher and true mentor.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'where', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Where's my toy car?
Where's Dad?

examples.text: А где машинка? Где моя машинка?
examples.trans: Hey, where's the toy car? Where's my toy car?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'better', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: It's better like this.
I feel better today.
Working. Making people's lives better.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'ставить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to put, to set up', paired with 'ставить'.

examples.text: Заходите. Поставьте, пожалуйста, правую ногу на кровать.
examples.trans: Come in. Please put your right foot on the bed.

examples.text: Поставьте, пожалуйста, правую ногу на кровать.
examples.trans: Please put your right foot on the bed.
Tomorrow we'll put on a latch.

meanings.note: Prefix 'об-' ('around, about') marks encirclement or comprehensive action (stem 'орудование'). Verbal action/result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание'. Common neuter noun meaning 'equipment, machinery' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Это договор на покупку строительного оборудования.
examples.trans: This is a contract for the purchase of construction equipment.
New equipment was delivered to the factory.

examples.text: А что у меня из оборудования?
examples.trans: And what equipment do I have?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'then, later, afterwards', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: First coffee, then work.
I'll call later.
And then waste will flow.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'говорить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to have a talk', paired with 'говорить'.

examples.trans: Talk to him.
We need to talk.

examples.text: Поговори с Аракеляном. Пусть он заберёт заявление.
examples.trans: Talk to Arakelyan. Get him to withdraw his statement.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What's this?
Look what I've got.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'here', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm here.
We live here.
But we're in business here.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to do, to make', paired with 'сделать'.

examples.trans: What are you doing?
I'm making dinner.
Hi, Arkady Borisovich. What are you doing?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Chef, I didn't take it.
I don't know.
There wasn't enough money.

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'вечать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to answer, to reply', paired with 'ответить'.

examples.text: Я вам звоню, а вы не отвечаете!
examples.trans: I call you, and you don't answer!

examples.text: Почему ты не отвечаешь на мои вопросы?
examples.trans: Why aren't you answering my questions?
Where is your uncle? Answer!

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'SMS, text message' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Alla Yevgenyevna immediately gets a text message.
Send me a text message.

examples.text: Я снимаю деньги с карточки. И Алла Евгеньевна сразу получает смс.
examples.trans: I withdraw money from my card. And Alla Yevgenyevna immediately gets a text message.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'well; come on', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Oh, come on, Dad!
Well?

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'тому').

examples.trans: Because I'm not a thief.

examples.text: Я устал, потому что много работал.
examples.trans: I'm tired because I worked a lot.
I'm at home because I'm ill.

meanings.note: Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'чего').

examples.text: Ты знаешь, что я хочу. Мне терять нечего.
examples.trans: You know what I want. I have nothing to lose.

examples.text: Павел Юрьевич, вам больше нечего сказать?
examples.trans: Pavel Yuryevich, do you have nothing more to say?
There was nothing left to ruin there!

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'ветить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to answer, to reply', paired with 'отвечать'.

examples.trans: I have to answer.
Answer me!

examples.text: Прости, я должен ответить. Да, Аллочка!
examples.trans: Sorry, I have to answer this. Yes, Allochka!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'so, then; like that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you?
That's good like that.
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'would', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Я бы на твоём месте подумал.
examples.trans: If I were you, I'd think about it.

examples.text: Юле бы дублёнку купили, Славику бы ноутбук.
examples.trans: We could have bought Yulia a sheepskin coat, and Slavik a laptop.
Look who's talking.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.
Dad and Mum.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'someone, somebody', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Finally someone is for the people!

examples.text: Слушай, тут пишут: «Гордость России! Наконец-то кто-то за народ!»
examples.trans: Listen, here they write: 'Pride of Russia! Finally someone is for the people!'

examples.text: Ты что, не понимаешь? Я задавить кого-то мог!
examples.trans: Don't you understand? I could have run someone over!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to wait, to expect', paired with 'подождать'.

examples.trans: Don't wait for me.
I'm waiting for you.
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?
